newsitem.title: UK: Dollar sturdy in late Europe, awaits Greenspan.
newsitem.headline: Dollar sturdy in late Europe, awaits Greenspan.

text.p: The dollar ended a quiet European session on a firm note, though dealers reported a slightly nervous atmosphere ahead of U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's closely-watched Humphrey-Hawkins testimony.

Early trading delivered a mild boost for the dollar in the shape of France's public sector audit, which was seen nurturing expectations of a punctual, broad-based start to European economic and monetary union (EMU) and so weighing on the mark.
But the U.S. currency wobbled slightly after Wall Street suffered a swift 50-point drop, sparking fears of a repeat performance of Friday's 130-point Dow Jones slide.

Analysts said the market was fearful Greenspan would trigger a sharp stock market decline, as he did in December when he warned investors against "irrational exuberance". U.S. stocks have roared ahead since then.

"There are a lot of rumours Greenspan might say something profound, particularly vis-a-vis the stock market...and that the stock market might collapse and the dollar might go with it," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy here.
The dollar was quoted at 1.7958/68 marks at 1534 GMT, off an earlier high of 1.7975 but up from 1.7883/88 in late Europe on Friday.
The Dow Jones industrial average stood at 7899.99, up 9.53 points or 0.12 percent from its previous close.

France's independent audit estimated the 1997 public deficit at 3.5-3.7 percent of GDP, above the EMU target of 3.0 but in line with market expectations. The government said tax hikes and spending cuts would lop 0.4 percent off the deficit.

That pressured the mark as the market again contemplated the prospect of a broad swathe of countries launching a weak euro in 1999. The mark fell to 3.3754/57 French francs and 972.60/90 Italian lire from Friday's closing levels of 3.3803/08 and 973.00/30.
Traders said dollar/mark would continue to struggle above the key psychological barrier of 1.80 marks.

"The general perception is that there's something or someone or some people above 1.80, and we think it's going to be very difficult for it to break through that," said Peter Heath, senior dealer at Merita Bank in London.

Dollar/yen snuggled in a modest half-yen range throughout the European session, with trade dampened by a holiday in Tokyo. It was quoted at 115.78/88 at 1550 GMT compared to 115.50/60 at the end of last week.

Fresh wobbles in Asian currency markets overnight, usually seen as dollar-supportive, had little impact on the U.S. currency. Dealers said Asian jitters had largely been discounted, and they were wary of support for the dollar eroding as those concerns subsided.
